papers.title: Wildfire, Restoration, and Postwildfire Rehabilitation Effects on Wind Erosion in the Great Basin
papers.abstract: Restoration of degraded areas and postdisturbance rehabilitation after wildfire encompass critical approaches for reducing and reversing impacts of wind erosion and sand and dust storms (SDS). However, the broad outcomes of dryland restoration and rehabilitation for wind erosion and SDS remain underexplored. Wind erosion is an emerging issue in the Great Basin of the western United States, exacerbated by invasive annual grasses and associated wildfire. Here, we assess potential wind erosion and SDS responses to wildfire, restoration, and postwildfire rehabilitation treatments at the regional scale in the Great Basin. We used 13 years of rangeland monitoring data, the Aeolian EROsion model, and the Land Treatment Digital Library to produce counterfactual model-predictions to estimate treatment effects. Our results, based on AERO model estimates of aeolian sediment flux, Q , revealed potential reductions across three management contexts compared to controls: 6.76 % decrease in Q in wildfire-affected regions, 54.3 and 58.0 % decrease in Q in for soil disturbance and aerial seeding restoration areas, and 49.8 to 56.0% decrease in Q in postwildfire rehabilitation treated sites. In particular, aerial seeding and soil disturbance restoration treatments, and postwildfire closure-treatments had higher perennial grass cover and the most decreased Q compared to untreated controls. These results represent an important regional scale assessment of wind erosion responses to restoration and postwildfire rehabilitation. Our findings underscore the application of integrating wind erosion and SDS mitigation into restoration and postdisturbance rehabilitation programs to provide land managers with strategies to reduce land degradation while fostering ecosystem resilience.

papers.title: Sagebrush Are Not Small Trees: Need and Considerations for Improved, Uniform Burn Severity Assessment in Shrub-Steppe Rangelands
papers.abstract: The introduction and proliferation of invasive annual grasses have increased wildfire size and frequency, contributing to the degradation of sagebrush steppe rangelands in the Great Basin of the western United States. The availability of timely and accurate burn severity data following a wildfire is critical for making well-informed postfire management decisions to address this degradation. However, most commonly used burn severity metrics were developed in the context of high biomass, high cover forested systems, which limits their utility in sagebrush steppe. The goal of this paper is to provide an overview of the current state of burn severity assessment in sagebrush steppe communities and to highlight areas for improvement. First, we compared common burn severity metrics, finding differences among them. We then assessed their utility in shrublands and found that most metrics fail to adequately capture key ecological conditions that drive postfire management decisions, such as perennial grass mortality or fine-scale heterogeneity in burn severity. Consequently, we advocate for the development of a standardized procedure that characterizes the state of the postburn plant community in the context of potential successional trajectories under different environmental and management scenarios. Finally, we provide a suite of ecological burn severity indicators that serve as a starting point in capturing the response of rangelands to fire. Most postfire restoration decisions and underlying burn severity estimates in rangelands are made during the weeks following wildfire. However, the effects of wildfire are not always readily apparent immediately after fire, necessitating an adaptive sampling procedure that allows for reassessment of site conditions and adjustments to management strategies. A standardized procedure designed specifically for rangelands is important because it will enable rapid assessment of the indicators relevant to postfire decision-making.

papers.title: Projected Global Mortality and Economic Burden from Wildfire Smoke under Climate Change
papers.abstract: Abstract Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of wildfires, amplifying landscape fire-sourced smoke (LFS), and its global health effects. However, future global LFS-attributable deaths and their associated attributable death costs remain poorly quantified. We projected global LFS-derived air pollution and the associated mortality and mortality-related economic burden from 2020 to 2100 under alternative climate and socioeconomic scenarios. We applied advanced deep learning algorithms trained on high-resolution, station-validated LFS data and bias-corrected climate projections to estimate daily LFS-derived fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and ozone (O3) concentrations at a 0.25° × 0.25° resolution under three Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). These projections were combined with future population, mortality, and value-of-statistical-life (VSL) estimates and LFS-adjusted exposure–response (E–R) relationships to quantify global, regional, and national all-cause mortality attributable to LFS and the corresponding economic costs of LFS-attributable deaths. We further identified the most affected regions and evaluated how LFS exposure and sociodemographic factors shape LFS-attributable death costs across SSPs. Climate change is projected to escalate LFS pollution and its attributable mortality burden, with annual attributable death costs reaching Int \$24.4 trillion (5.52 million deaths) by 2100 under a high-emission (SSP3–7.0) scenario. In contrast, a low-emission (SSP1–2.6) pathway could reduce attributable mortality by 40.5%, preventing 2.24 million deaths annually and saving Int \$5.9 trillion by 2100. Regional disparities are expected, with some high-income regions, such as Europe, showing declines in LFS levels and associated mortality, while low- and middle-income countries are projected to remain disproportionately vulnerable to elevated LFS exposure and attributable death costs. Projected global LFS exposure is expected to increase even under a low-emission pathway, while LFS-attributable deaths and VSL-based attributable death costs vary substantially across the SSPs. These differences reflect the combined effects of changes in the LFS exposure, demographic shifts, baseline mortality, and economic development. Our findings highlight LFS-derived air pollution as an increasingly consequential health hazard and underscore the potential health and economic benefits of sustainable development, low-emission pathways, and effective climate mitigation.

papers.title: Brittle by Design? Multi-Scenario Reinforcement Learning for Robust Mission Coordination in Systems of Systems
papers.abstract: As systems engineering (SE) shifts from monolithic systems to Systems of Systems, Mission Engineering (ME) has emerged as a new line of thinking in SE. Mission environments are uncertain and dynamic, and outcomes depend on how mission assets interact with them, rendering static architectures brittle and calling for flexible yet analytically rigorous ME approaches. We propose an intelligent mission coordination methodology integrating high-fidelity digital mission models with Reinforcement Learning (RL) for adaptive task allocation. Using a Digital Engineering (DE) infrastructure comprising a digital mission model and agent-based simulation, we formulate mission tactics management as a Markov Decision Process and train an RL coordinator with Proximal Policy Optimization to map mission states to tactical actions from realized outcomes. An aerial firefighting mission with three scenarios demonstrates the approach. First, all trained coordinators significantly outperform random and heuristic baselines. Second, single-scenario coordinators can be brittle: the coordinator trained on the more forgiving scenario degrades to random tactics performance in more demanding scenarios, whereas the demanding-scenario coordinator retains most of its advantage when transferred. Third, within the same training budget, a coordinator trained on both scenarios concurrently matches the scenario-specific coordinators in their own scenarios and significantly outperforms every other policy. Sensitivity analyses on ignition location, weather, scenario, and training curricula show that the variability represented during training shapes post-deployment performance. This proof of concept shows DE-enabled mission simulations combined with RL offer a reusable methodology for improving ME practice, which can be extended to fleet design and selection from a mission-first perspective.

papers.title: Heathland above-ground biomass estimation using UAV and LiDAR
papers.abstract: 1. Heathland is an important carbon sink and habitat for biodiversity. It is heavily managed Heathland is an important carbon sink and habitat for biodiversity. It is heavily managed through grazing and prescribed fire and faces increasing threats from wildfire and forest encroachment. Because the proportion of overall heathland carbon stock is predominately below-ground, above-ground biomass (AGB) is often neglected. Quantifying both AGB and soil organic carbon (SOC) is therefore important for understanding total heathland carbon storage. 2. This study was conducted at Thursley National Nature Reserve, UK. We evaluated the effectiveness of hand-held Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) Structure-from-Motion (SfM) for estimating above-ground biomass (AGB) and associated carbon stocks across dry (Calluna vulgaris) and wet (Erica tetralix) heathlands with different stand ages and fire histories. Vegetation was scanned before destructive biomass sampling, and the resulting three-dimensional (3D) point clouds were processed to derive structural metrics using canopy height models (CHMs) and voxelization. These metrics were then used to develop and evaluate regression models for AGB estimation, calibrated against the destructively sampled AGB. 3. In dry heathland, C. vulgaris stands aged 5, 19 and over 25 years had 95th-percentile canopy heights (H95) of 0.27 ± 0.01, 0.46 ± 0.04 and 0.76 ± 0.05 m, respectively, and AGB of 5.01 ± 0.55, 14.31 ± 2.19 and 31.92 ± 2.20 t ha⁻¹, respectively. Volumetric metrics provided better model fits than canopy height alone, with optimal resolutions of 20 mm for LiDAR voxel-derived and SfM CHM-derived volume, and 5 mm for LiDAR CHM-derived volume. LiDAR-derived models showed little evidence that biomass–structure relationships differed between C. vulgaris-dominated dry and E. tetralix-dominated wet heath, whereas the height-based model showed marginal evidence of heath-type-dependent relationships. 4. SOC were significantly greater in older dry (81.52±9.99 t ha⁻¹) than younger dry heath (56.08±6.27 t ha⁻¹) and were highest in wet heath (181.97±28.08 t ha⁻¹). Synthesis and applications: Three-dimensional structural metrics provide a non-destructive approach for monitoring AGB and associated carbon stocks in lowland heathlands. This method could enable repeated assessments of vegetation structure and biomass in response to management, while soil carbon measurements highlight the importance of considering below-ground carbon storage when evaluating heathland management strategies.

papers.title: Back in the wild: where reintroduced California Condors spend their time
papers.abstract: Captive breeding and reintroduction programmes have been instrumental in preventing the extinction of critically endangered species. As these efforts advance towards recovering self‐sustaining wild populations, understanding how reintroduced animals use space is essential for long‐term success. Home‐range analyses provide insight into habitat use, behavioural flexibility and exposure to human‐related threats, which are key for adaptive management. We compared annual home‐ranges of 12 California Condors Gymnogyps californianus tracked from 2016 to 2020 at two ecologically distinct release sites: the fragmented, urban‐influenced landscapes of southern California and the more heterogeneous coastal habitats of central California. Annual autocorrelated kernel density estimation (AKDE) home‐range estimates were approximately 3.44 times as large in southern California Condors (c. 8444.93 km 2 ) as in central California Condors (c. 2246 km 2 ), suggesting regional differences in habitat fragmentation, resource distribution and topography. Although absolute variability was greater in southern California, central California Condors showed greater relative variability in space use, consistent with diverse foraging opportunities across inland and coastal environments. These findings demonstrate how regional landscape characteristics influence condor movement patterns and emphasize the importance of site‐specific management, including maintaining connectivity in southern California and monitoring inland and coastal resources in the central population.

papers.title: Global gridded data for the Shared Socio-economic Pathways
papers.abstract: The shared socio-economic pathways (SSPs) provide storylines for plausible future global developments under a consistent set of assumptions. Primarily, the SSPs have been used to derive quantitative scenarios of greenhouse gas emissions for use in general circulation models and other large-scale, physically based models of environmental change. Their use in large-scale socio-environmental simulation modelling has been less forthcoming. Behavioural models of land systems, typically operating within agent-based frameworks, attempt to explicitly represent the varied socio-environmental factors that characterise the SSP storylines. Such simulation models are often geospatial and grid-based, capable of representing dynamics at resolutions of up to 10s km2 over large extents (continental to global). However, such approaches demand geospatial (usually gridded) input data for multiple social and human variables - often together known as capitals - such as education levels and infrastructure. The lack of such input data for the future SSP storylines has been a substantial limitation in the application of large-scale behavioural models of land systems specifically and of socio-environmental modelling more generally. Here, we present global gridded data for socio-economic capitals useful for simulation models and consistent with the SSP storylines, disaggregated spatially to a 0.25o grid. We analyse the spatial and temporal characteristics of the projected data, comparing them to projections of GDP, and discuss their utility and limitations for large-scale socio-environmental modelling.

papers.title: Resilience of standalone microgrids: indicators, enhancement strategies, and challenges—an integrative review
papers.abstract: Microgrids have emerged as a promising solution for improving energy access, enhancing local energy independence, and strengthening resilience against environmental, technical, and operational disturbances. Resilience refers to the ability of a system to withstand, adapt to, and recover from disruptive events while maintaining reliable operation. Unlike grid-connected systems, standalone or islanded microgrids must operate autonomously during disturbances, making resilience a critical design and operational consideration. This paper presents an integrative review of the state-of-the-art (SOTA) strategies, indicators, and challenges associated with enhancing the resilience of standalone microgrids. Following a PRISMA-guided review methodology, the study synthesizes 60 primary studies published between 2014 and 2025, supported by 28 contextual references. Coding of the primary studies shows that 95% rely on simulation or analytical modeling, with only three reporting experimental or hardware-in-the-loop validation, which remains the principal limitation of the current evidence base. The discussion is categorized into four major areas: design and planning, control strategies, energy management, and protection systems. In addition, the review examines resilience assessment metrics and emerging cyber-physical resilience approaches for modern standalone microgrids. The paper further identifies major technical, economic, environmental, and regulatory challenges affecting the operation of resilient microgrids, including protection coordination, renewable intermittency, communication dependence, cybersecurity risks, economic limitations, and vulnerability to extreme weather events. Various resilience enhancement approaches—distributed energy resource diversification, adaptive reconfiguration, hierarchical control, predictive energy management, and the interconnection of neighboring standalone microgrids—are critically analyzed to provide a broader understanding of resilient standalone microgrid development. Finally, the review highlights important research gaps and future directions, including the need for standardized resilience metrics, integrated cyber-physical security frameworks, climate-adaptive planning models, and practical implementation strategies. Although significant progress has been achieved in microgrid modeling, control, and optimization, considerable challenges remain in bridging theoretical research with large-scale real-world deployment of resilient standalone microgrids.

papers.title: Recovering Plausible Transmission Outage Scenarios
papers.abstract: Expansion planning for extreme weather needs outage scenarios that specify which transmission branches fail. However, public outage records often only report customers without power by county, making it unclear how to exploit this information to create outage scenarios. We propose a method to recover sets of outaged branches that most closely match regional load shed data. This gives us sets of plausible outages for a given hazard event. We formulate a bilevel problem with a load shedding DC optimal power flow in the lower level. We relax the binary branch states to differentiate the lower level problem, replace it with its sensitivity matrix, and use gradient descent to update the upper level. We treat the relaxed branch states as probabilities and perform randomized rounding to restore integrality. On three test systems with synthetic outages, the recovered sets reduce the load shed error to $0.02-4.5\%$. On the California Test System with storm data from December 2025, the error falls to $23\%$. These scenarios give expansion planning a reliable source of outage data tied to observed hazards.

papers.title: The Crowd: Zooming in on Social Behaviour
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The direct observation of social behaviour has almost completely vanished from socialpsychological research, in favour of studies of attitudes, identities and cognitions. Using crowd psychology as an illustration, this article argues for a renewed focus on observational research enabled by recent technological advances, including high‐resolution video, motion tracking, eye tracking and large‐scale crowd experiments. We review the historical development of crowd research in social psychology, sociology and physics, highlighting how dominant theories have focused on exceptional phenomena, such as riots, panic and crowd violence whilst relying heavily on self‐reports and retrospective accounts. Using recent observational research as an example, the article shows that everyday crowds are characterised by substantial behavioural heterogeneity, limited contagion effects and highly coordinated collective behaviour. These findings challenge established social psychological crowd theories, thereby demonstrating that using these methods is very worthwhile. We conclude that interdisciplinary observational approaches offer powerful opportunities for social psychology to study real‐world social interaction and to develop theories that better account for spatial, material and dynamic social processes.

papers.title: Characteristics of size-resolved organic aerosols using offline aerosol mass spectrometry: NYC-METS
papers.abstract: To study the size-resolved organic aerosol composition in New York City, daily aerosol samples were collected using a Micro-Orifice Uniform Deposition Impactor (MOUDI) during the Summer 2023 New York City Metropolitan Measurements of Emissions and TransformationS (NYC-METS) campaign. Organic aerosol mass loading, size distribution, composition, and elemental ratios were measured using offline analysis with a High-Resolution Time-of-Flight Aerosol Mass Spectrometer (HR-TOF-AMS). Most organic aerosol mass was found in the size range of 0.32–0.56 µm and a unimodal size distribution was observed (0.056–5.6 µm). Higher aerosol mass loadings were observed under fire and hazy conditions compared to cleaner conditions. Across all conditions, more highly oxidized species (CHO and CHOx) were found in the 0.18–1 µm size range. A novel method for functional group quantification from AMS data was applied. This showed a higher percentage of carboxylic acid groups on stages 6–8 (0.18–1 µm) which suggests more extensive secondary organic aerosol formation or aging processes influencing that size range. The offline-AMS results were compared to measurements from an in situ online-AMS and both datasets exhibited similar trends in the mass concentrations with time and composition. However, for aerosol samples collected during fire and hazy conditions, some volatile components were likely lost before offline sample analysis, leading to higher oxygen-to-carbon (O/C) ratios in the offline measurements. The combination of MOUDI with the offline-AMS provides unique insights into the size-resolved composition of organic aerosol particles in New York City.

papers.title: Can Clean-Tech Patents and Energy Productivity Enhance Carbon Productivity in a Fossil Fuel Exporting Economy? Lessons from Australia
papers.abstract: Within the concept of sustainable development, economic growth should be driven by low-carbon practices and improved carbon productivity. While several studies have focused on low-carbon economy delivery, little has been done on carbon productivity and its relationship with innovative green technologies. This study assesses the effect of green-tech patents and energy productivity on the carbon productivity of Australia using the ARDL long run form and bounds test between 1990 and 2020. The Westerlund’s variance ratio cointegration estimates indicate that all variables are integrated. The ARDL long-form and bounds estimates indicate that both green-tech patents and energy productivity help in the delivery of low-carbon productivity in Australia. The ARDL long form estimates further suggest that rising economic growth hinders improvements in carbon productivity levels of the Australian economy. Finally, the empirical outcomes of the Toda-Yamamoto test indicate (i) a one-directional causality from green-tech patents to both energy and carbon productivity; (ii) a rebound causal effect between economic growth and carbon productivity. For policy suggestions, the government of Australia could heavily invest in innovations in environmental technologies to improve carbon productivity levels and to determine progress towards reducing climate change by supporting corporations to consider carbon as a useful component and not a waste product. Second, the government could ground the carbon productivity concept in its commitments to reducing fossil carbon consumption. Corporations that perform well in delivering carbon dioxide emissions productivity could benefit from tax incentives and government grants. Finally, given that rising economic growth reduces or improves the Australian economy’s carbon productivity levels, the government could institute non-monetary awards for individuals or corporations with strong records of registered green-tech patents and green energy technologies.

papers.title: A comprehensive checklist of North American gypsophile plants: insights into their distribution and state of knowledge
papers.abstract: Background and aims – We present the first comprehensive checklist of North American gypsophiles (plants restricted or nearly restricted to gypsum soils) to encourage the further exploration of gypsum exposures, promote systematic studies, and raise awareness about the potential need of conservation measures for these ecologically and evolutionary unique species. Material and methods – The checklist was based on a historical literature search, herbarium specimens, and fieldwork. We estimated an Aridity Index for the gypsum localities of all occurrences, taxa description over time, growth form, generic diversity within families as compared to global patterns, and conservation status. Key results – We recognize 287 taxa as gypsophiles, which occur from Montana, USA to southern Mexico, including 282 angiosperm taxa, 3 ferns, one gymnosperm, and one lycophyte. Herbaria and literature review retrieved 3,528 records for gypsophile taxa. The gypsum localities from these records were classified from arid to humid, with most being arid or semi-arid. The most diverse families were Asteraceae (77 taxa), Brassicaceae (14), Loasaceae/Nyctaginaceae (13), and Cactaceae/Namaceae (11). The most diverse genera were Mentzelia / Nama / Nerisyrenia (11), Phacelia / Pinguicula (9), and Drymaria / Gaillardia (8). Most gypsophile taxa were classified as perennial herbs (207) or shrubs (38), but annual herbs (17) and one tree-like species were also recorded. Only 45 taxa were found to be protected at any level. Conclusion – North America has the most diverse gypsophile flora yet known globally. It is composed of a wide phylogenetic diversity including many growth forms and biomes, ranging from xeric shrublands to grasslands, coniferous forests, and tropical forests. Few gypsophile taxa have legal protections, and additional studies are clearly needed to assess their conservation risk. This first comprehensive checklist, while subject to change, will serve as a foundation for future research.

papers.title: From innovation to implementation: a global scoping review of artificial intelligence applications, governance, and challenges in humanitarian contexts
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a tool for supporting humanitarian action through hazards and crisis prediction, real time monitoring of evolving crisis conditions and humanitarian needs, resource allocation, and decision-making. However, evidence on how AI is implemented, evaluated, and governed across humanitarian contexts remains fragmented. In this scoping review, we mapped the global evidence on the application of AI in humanitarian settings, including its distribution across the emergency management cycle, deployment maturity, and evaluation. We also identified any governance considerations, as well as enabling factors for and challenges to its implementation, with particular attention to the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, Gulf Cooperation Council countries (GCC), and Qatar. Methods: The methodology of this scoping review followed the framework set by Arksey and O'Malley, which comprises the formulation of the research question, selection of records, data charting, and synthesis of findings. We searched six databases (ProQuest, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus), queried Google Scholar, and ran targeted grey literature searches through the webpages of major humanitarian organisations for records reporting on the application, implementation, or governance of AI in humanitarian contexts. We descriptively and narratively synthesised the extracted data. Results: We included 57 scholarly publications and 17 grey literature reports. Application of AI was most frequently reported in sudden-onset natural disasters, particularly floods and earthquakes, and was commonly used to support disaster monitoring, crisis informatics, search-and-rescue, logistics optimisation, hazard prediction, and geospatial analysis. Deep learning and machine learning were the most common model families. Across the emergency management cycle, most applications of AI focused on preparedness and response, while recovery was rarely addressed. Geographically, most evidence originated from Asia, while research from the MENA and GCC regions remained limited. Most reported systems remained prototypes or retrospectively validated models, with relatively few seeing operational deployment or field implementation. Governance issues were discussed more extensively in grey literature than in scholarly publications. Community participation, equity considerations, and formal governance frameworks were inconsistently reported. Conclusions: AI is increasingly being applied in humanitarian contexts, but it is heterogeneously distributed across regions, humanitarian contexts, and emergency management. Greater emphasis is needed on real-world deployment, implementation-focused evaluation, participatory approaches, and governance frameworks that support responsible, equitable, and context-sensitive AI adoption.

papers.title: Developing a Climate Impact Indicator Framework for the UK Agri‐Food Sector: A Literature Review and Stakeholder Co‐Production Approach
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Consistent monitoring and reporting of the impacts of weather in a changing climate is a key component in being able to attribute future risk and losses to weather variations. This allows the production of evidence required to facilitate mitigation, adaptation strategies and influence policy implementation. The agri‐food sector has always been impacted by weather and climate, but whilst data are consistently produced for metrics relating to the sector, there is no consistent reporting of how weather and climate are influencing these. This paper describes the foundation of a new proposed annual report, being produced for the Royal Meteorological Society's State of the Climate for the UK Agri‐Food Sector project in partnership with Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and UK Met Office. We identify and detail the ways in which weather has affected the agri‐food sector, comprising of a literature and data review and outputs of a co‐production workshop with experts from across the sector. We then provide a summary of the quantitative impact indicators that will be used in the future report, which look at Water, Crop Suitability, Disease and Pest, Extreme Events and Price and Yields, outlining how they are being produced, and the rationale behind them.

papers.title: Estimating local economic impacts on remote Indigenous communities with adapted input–output models
papers.abstract: The limited community-level data and the lack of economic models tailored to Indigenous economies present significant challenges for conducting ex-ante evaluations of investments in remote Indigenous communities. This lack of adequate modelling efforts might result in misleading government interventions that could have limited or even negative economic impacts for the communities concerned. This study develops a methodological tool to support policy and government planning through Input-Output models adapted to capture the structure of local economies in remote Indigenous communities in Canada. Adapting the Northwest Territories Supply and Use Tables (240 industries and 492 products) published by Statistics Canada, the model incorporates community-specific sectors, leakages, imports, transportation costs, inventories and commercial activities. Using Fort McPherson, Northwest Territories, as a case study, we estimate the economic impacts of community-based biomass energy production, including potential cost savings, business creation and greater income circulation. Results show positive local effects: the biomass project generates total sector output of CAD 602,021 (output multiplier of 1.023). Total household income impacts reach CAD 86,498, comprising CAD 57,618 from the disposable-income effect of lower energy costs and CAD 28,880 in wage income from project-related sectoral activity. Average output multipliers in Fort McPherson (1.03) were substantially lower than comparable territorial multipliers (1.40), highlighting the importance of community-specific modelling. Sensitivity analysis showed that total sector output varied by only 1.03% across alternative household spending retention assumptions. This methodology can be applied to other remote and marginalised communities, providing a framework to guide local investments, energy security and economic development.

papers.title: From evidence to action: a narrative literature review to inform cross-border one health implementation in the Kavango-Zambezi region
papers.abstract: Introduction Despite growing commitment to One Health, there is limited operational guidance for implementing cross-border approaches in transboundary regions. The Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area (KAZA-TFCA), spanning the Southern African countries of Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, faces interconnected challenges at the human-animal-environment interface, including zoonotic disease risks, food insecurity, environmental change, and complex governance. This study synthesises evidence to identify barriers and opportunities for operationalising One Health across KAZA.Theory This narrative review is informed by the One Health framework, which recognises the interdependence of human, animal and environmental health, and draws on a systems perspective to examine cross-border governance, multisectoral collaboration, and community participation in transboundary settings.Method A narrative review, following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, was conducted of studies published between 2010 and 2024 across nine databases. Thirty-eight studies were thematically synthesised and analysed across six domains: animal health, food security, environmental health, governance, community perceptions, and health and veterinary services.Results Findings show that challenges are driven by cross-border policy fragmentation, disjointed surveillance coordination, unequal resource access, and limited community inclusion in decision-making. Environmental pressures such as climate variability, land-use change, and water scarcity exacerbate vulnerabilities across sectors. Community trust and participation are central to effective implementation but remain under-addressed.Discussion An evidence-informed framework is proposed for cross-border One Health implementation that is centred on policy harmonisation, integrated planning, inclusive governance, and meaningful community engagement. These insights are relevant to other transboundary regions facing similar challenges and highlight the need for coordinated, equity-focused strategies to translate policy into action.

papers.title: Downstream industrial investment in a proposed Special Economic Zone: an ex-ante conditional CGE appraisal of Mekar Putih, South Kalimantan, Indonesia
papers.abstract: This study assesses the conditional economy-wide impacts of downstream industrial investment associated with the proposed Mekar Putih Special Economic Zone in South Kalimantan, Indonesia. A 10-sector regional computable general equilibrium (CGE) model uses a RAS-updated input–output database with hybrid cell injection for emerging nickel and silica processing. Investment, export-capacity, and productivity shocks represent assumed additions to the baseline rather than evidence that the zone will attract investment. Under the main scenario (S3), an annual investment injection of IDR 108 trillion increases provincial gross regional domestic product (GRDP) by 15.94% and generates approximately 84,900 jobs. At 50% additionality, the GRDP gain declines to about 7.8%. Comparison with the proponent’s feasibility study suggests a medium-term GRDP gain of approximately 8–12%, conditional on investment realisation. The full value-chain scenario (S5) yields 49.85%, illustrating an upper bound rather than a forecast. Normalised GRDP responses of 0.147–0.185 percentage points per trillion rupiah indicate that differences across scenarios largely reflect investment scale. District-level effects are allocated top-down. These estimates should not be interpreted as net welfare gains.

papers.title: Land-based climate policy, land prices, and the green transition trilemma: Evidence from Bolivia
papers.abstract: Land-based climate policies in forest-rich developing economies are often assessed separately, overlooking how land scarcity, land prices, and macroeconomic constraints shape feasibility. This paper examines the macro-financial challenges of sustainable agriculture and forest conservation in Bolivia, where deforestation is high and fiscal and external constraints bind. We develop a dynamic version of the Exposure to Structural Transformation in an Ecologic-Economic Model (D-ESTEEM) to jointly analyse Bolivia's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) policies for forest conservation and agricultural productivity. The locally calibrated, environmentally extended input-output model combines continuous-time monetary system dynamics, endogenous land prices, and demand-led adjustments in a small open economy. Forest conservation reduces environmental pressures but raises land prices, weakening the competitiveness of land-intensive activities and worsening fiscal and balance-of-payments pressures. Agricultural productivity measures ease land pressures and support output but rely on imported inputs, reinforcing external dependence. Overall, the NDCs improve economic activity and environmental outcomes while worsening fiscal and trade imbalances. Fiscal consolidation and exchange-rate adjustment mitigate some imbalances but entail inflationary pressures or lower output and employment. Environmental gains may therefore come at the cost of macroeconomic fragility. The paper shows how conservation-induced land scarcity and land price dynamics interact with fiscal and balance-of-payments constraints to determine the feasibility of land-based transitions in resource-dependent economies.

papers.title: Supporting post-bushfire biodiversity through citizen science tourism: recovery, regeneration, and reflections
papers.abstract: The Australian 2019–20 Black Summer bushfires had profound ecological and socio-economic impacts on Kangaroo Island, threatening iconic species including koalas, Kangaroo Island dunnarts, and glossy black cockatoos, and disrupting local tourism. In response, and co-designed with multiple stakeholders, Passport to Recovery (P2R) was developed as a tourist-focused, place-based citizen science program to quickly integrate multiple biodiversity monitoring projects into a single, cohesive experience. Since its inception, over 5,000 tourists have participated, generating datasets that have informed post-fire ecological restoration and local conservation decision-making. Our findings reveal that P2R was effective in attracting both new and experienced citizen scientists, indicating that our novel model of cross-sectoral, multi-benefit citizen science could be utilised in other peri- or post-environmental disaster settings to produce ecological data. Our findings also consider how tourist-focused programs can support the broader recovery of local businesses by positioning citizen science as a tourism experience, despite incentives not being highly effective. We conclude by reflecting on the shortcomings of our design approach and offer important insights into the challenges that can emerge or persist, including mobile app coverage, and the idiosyncrasies of managing 12 contrasting projects underpinned by different methodologies and in partnership with multiple stakeholders.
